Title: A New Attorney General, a Vaccine Order, and a President Who Won't Say No to Emergency Powers
Content:
In one week: Trump's personal lawyer took over the Justice Department, the president rewrote childhood vaccine policy by fiat, ICE moved to arm agents with shock gloves, and courts pushed back on the White House ballroom and Kennedy Center takeover — even as Trump's approval sank to 33 percent.

```markdown The week of August 8 through 14 unfolded as a study in contrasts: an administration consolidating personal control over the machinery of government even as courts, career officials, and public opinion pushed back at nearly every turn. By week's end, a president who had installed his own former defense lawyer atop the Justice Department was also facing a 33 percent approval rating, a defeated lawsuit against Harvard, and a blocked construction project he could not simply will into existence.

The week opened with the Senate's confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general, a 50-49 vote that required a Republican tiebreaker to succeed. Blanche had defended Trump personally in his criminal cases before serving as acting attorney general, and critics saw his elevation — following his role in the second indictment of James Comey and a contested "anti-weaponization fund" — as confirmation that the Justice Department's traditional independence from the White House had effectively ended. The pattern did not stay abstract for long: within the same weekend, Trump publicly attacked U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro for dropping charges against Olympian David Hearn after her office determined that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool had resulted from faulty installation, not vandalism. Trump demanded Pirro reverse the decision and insulted both Hearn and his attorney — a rare instance of a president publicly pressuring a specific prosecutor over a specific case involving a private citizen.

The weekend also brought discouraging economic news. The Department of Labor reported a loss of 23,000 jobs in July, with sharp downward revisions to prior months, while polling showed inflation concerns had climbed sharply since 2024, with women accounting for a disproportionate share of workers leaving the labor force. Elsewhere, a D.C. Circuit panel ruled that Trump lacked unilateral authority to build a ballroom on White House grounds without congressional approval, rejecting the administration's national security justification; Trump vowed to appeal. And in Texas, bulldozers arrived at Big Bend National Park to begin border wall construction after the administration waived dozens of environmental and cultural protection laws — despite the area recording only about 100 to 125 unlawful crossings a year.

By Monday, the week's defining executive action arrived: Trump signed an order directing the Department of Health and Human Services to reduce the recommended childhood vaccine schedule, split the MMR shot into three separate doses, and instructed the attorney general to challenge state vaccine mandates. The order bypassed the CDC's normal scientific review process and revived a policy previously blocked in court. At the signing, Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. repeated unproven claims linking vaccines to autism; Louisiana Senator Bill Cassidy, a physician, publicly objected. The same day, the Justice Department unveiled $300 million in "Model Cities" policing grants conditioned on cities adopting federal immigration enforcement and specific homelessness policies — terms several Democratic-led cities declined outright. DHS quietly published a procurement notice seeking up to $20 million for electric-shock gloves for ICE agents, despite manufacturer warnings against their use on vulnerable populations and past deaths linked to similar devices in custody. Monday also brought a North Carolina bill letting the state Supreme Court's Republican majority remove judges without independent review, and reporting that the National Park Service had diverted $323 million to White House grounds even as the Interior Secretary acknowledged a $30 billion nationwide park maintenance backlog. At an ICE facility in Mississippi, detainees reported a gas leak followed by denial of medical care, then a two-day power outage without air conditioning during extreme heat.

Tuesday shifted focus to immigration enforcement's reach into political expression. The State Department disclosed it had revoked more than 175,000 visas since Trump took office — four times the pace under the Biden administration — including cases tied to political commentary, a Turkish student's op-ed on Gaza, and parents seeking birthright citizenship for their children. The same day, reporting revealed that Trump had secretly left Turkey earlier in the month via a catering truck and decoy Air Force One, prompted by a low-confidence CIA assessment of an Iranian assassination threat; he took indicted aide Walt Nauta with him while leaving Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the traveling press pool behind as decoys. The pressure campaign against Pirro's office escalated further, with the White House formally asking Justice Department headquarters to consider new charges against Hearn — an extraordinary departure from the arm's-length relationship prosecutors are supposed to maintain from the White House. Separately, the Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion expanding executive privilege to cover communications between the president and outside advisors, with clear implications for congressional oversight should Democrats retake the House. Reporting also detailed Jared Kushner's purchase of disputed Albanian resort property from a man later accused of drug trafficking, and disclosed that Kushner's private firm had collected substantial fees from governments he was simultaneously negotiating with on the government's behalf. And a watchdog analysis found that Justice Samuel Alito had gained up to $2.9 million from oil and gas holdings as the Supreme Court prepared to hear a climate liability case; calls for his recusal were rejected.

Wednesday brought the week's clearest accounting of presidential enrichment. Investigations documented Trump personally earning roughly $2.2 billion through cryptocurrency ventures, a Truth Social pay-for-access scheme, a $10 billion IRS settlement, and a $400 million plane gift from Qatar, while a UAE-backed $2 billion investment flowed through his World Liberty Financial venture into Binance despite that exchange's history of money-laundering violations. That same day, Intercept Media and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump over "Truth API," a $100,000-per-month subscription service giving Wall Street firms early access to the president's posts — arguing the arrangement violates equal-access and First Amendment principles governing official government communications. Compounding the financial throughline, Treasury and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network permanently repealed the requirement for companies to report beneficial ownership information and ordered the deletion of already-collected data, reversing a 2020 law designed to combat money laundering by traffickers and kleptocrats. Against this backdrop, a new poll showed Trump's approval falling to 33 percent, with 60 percent of respondents saying he was not honest and trustworthy and 53 percent describing him as too old for the office; a former White House cardiologist publicly questioned his health and fitness to serve. The Justice Department also arrested Heidi Beirich, a prominent former Southern Poverty Law Center executive and extremism researcher, on financial charges her attorney called retaliatory. And press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced she would resign at the end of the month after nearly two years marked by restricted press access, the exclusion of the Associated Press, and a documented pattern of falsehoods.

Thursday tested whether court orders could actually constrain the administration's allies. The Kennedy Center's Trump-aligned board voted to inscribe his name on the building and proceed with a closure plan despite a federal judge's ruling blocking both actions — open defiance of a court order rather than mere resistance to one. The same day, Judge Richard Stearns dismissed the administration's antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard, finding it failed to plausibly allege an ongoing civil rights violation, constraining one avenue the administration had used to pressure universities. Court documents also revealed "Operation Puppet Master," a federal surveillance effort that had infiltrated meetings of progressive organizations, labor unions, and anti-ICE protest groups in Minnesota using undercover officers, chat monitoring, and license plate tracking; fifteen defendants faced federal charges. HHS finalized a rule eliminating Medicaid and CHIP coverage for gender-affirming care for transgender youth, despite roughly 90 percent of nearly 35,000 public comments opposing the change. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth briefed only Republican lawmakers on a proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget, withholding information about Caribbean boat strikes and the decoy Air Force One flight — prompting Republican Senator Thom Tillis to warn the approach could doom bipartisan passage. And Trump signed a memorandum ordering the Navy to revert to steam catapults on a nearly finished aircraft carrier, overriding objections from Navy officials and the system's contractor over cost and schedule risk.

The week closed on Friday with the administration formally asking the Supreme Court to stay the appeals court ruling against the White House ballroom, arguing the project was essential to national security — setting up a direct test of whether the Court would back the executive branch's claim to unilateral authority over public property. In the week's most striking moment regarding electoral process, Trump, prompted by a sympathetic radio host who suggested declaring a national security emergency to impose new voter ID, citizenship, and mail-ballot restrictions, responded only that "stranger things have happened," declining to disavow the idea. ICE and the Transportation Security Administration meanwhile began coordinating airport arrests of individuals with expired visas, including people holding valid work permits awaiting extensions, aiming for roughly 2,000 daily arrests under an expanded definition treating all overstays as criminal — continuing the week's arc from ankle monitors and shock gloves toward broader enforcement authority. Economic indicators darkened further: retail sales fell 0.6 percent against a forecast of 0.1 percent growth, and gas prices hit a record high for the date even as Trump described the economy as strong only "from the standpoint of Wall Street." Two smaller but notable developments closed the week: Columbus, Ohio restricted its police department's sharing of license-plate surveillance data statewide after a public hearing revealed over 15,000 searches potentially tied to immigration enforcement, and Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges in the killing of a healthcare executive, with sentencing set for December.

Taken as a whole, the week captured a government moving in two directions simultaneously. The confirmation of a former personal lawyer as the nation's top law enforcement officer, sustained pressure on an independent prosecutor, a unilateral rewrite of vaccine policy, and the accumulation of personal financial gain from the presidency all point toward power concentrating in the hands of one man with fewer internal checks willing or able to resist him. Yet the same week produced an appellate defeat on the ballroom, a dismissed lawsuit against Harvard, a lawsuit challenging pay-for-access presidential communications, and an approval rating scraping historic lows — evidence that courts, career institutions, and public opinion remain functioning, if strained, counterweights. Whether that resistance holds, or whether defiance of court orders at places like the Kennedy Center becomes the template rather than the exception, is a question this week left open rather than settled. ```
Excerpt: This week combined institutional capture with institutional resistance.

Title: This Week in Democracy: A President Who Answers to No One
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which the machinery meant to check presidential power kept declining to use it — even as other parts of that same machinery pushed back hard enough to show the difference was a choice, not an inevitability.

**The Weekend**

The week opened with Attorney General Todd Blanche telling a national television audience that no attorney general should promise to act independently of the president. The remark came just days after his narrow confirmation, which followed the dismissal of his predecessor for insufficient action against Trump's political opponents. It set the tone for a week in which the country's central law-enforcement and regulatory bodies were repeatedly asked, directly or through their actions, whether they served the presidency or the public — and answered in ways that varied sharply depending on which institution was doing the answering.

That same weekend brought a wave of reporting on the immigration court system, where due process appeared to be eroding on several fronts at once. ICE agents made arrests inside courthouses despite the system's long-recognized chilling effect on attendance. "Mega master" hearings, sometimes scheduled with as little as fifteen days' notice, produced more than 53,000 in-absentia removal orders in June alone. More than 100 sitting immigration judges have been replaced by new appointees marketed as "deportation judges," who now grant relief in fewer than 2 percent of the cases they hear. A separate Texas Tribune analysis found children held well beyond the legally mandated 20-day detention limit. Taken together, these findings described a system built increasingly to produce removals rather than adjudicate them.

Financial self-dealing surfaced on multiple fronts over the same weekend. General Dynamics was found to have kept $533 million for an artillery factory that never became functional, with no accountability attached. House Democrats opened an insider-trading investigation after an Energy Fuels executive purchased company stock shortly before a monument-shrinkage decision that benefited the firm. And federal regulators approved a bank charter for World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's cryptocurrency venture, which has already funneled more than $1.6 billion to the family. The president, meanwhile, staged a photo-op crediting himself for a drop in drug prices actually driven by a Biden-era law, and separately claimed inflation was falling and that the United States "totally controls" the Strait of Hormuz — both claims contradicted by available data.

**Monday**

The judiciary offered a more mixed picture. The Supreme Court declined to rehear Trump's appeal in the E. Jean Carroll case, leaving intact the $5 million jury verdict finding him liable for sexual abuse and defamation — a quiet but firm assertion that a jury's finding against a sitting president cannot simply be undone by petition. A federal judge separately blocked the FBI and General Services Administration's plan to relocate FBI headquarters to the Reagan Building, ruling that the $555 million reprogramming exceeded statutory authority and permanently enjoining the agencies from proceeding.

That same day, ABC filed a federal lawsuit against the FCC and its chair, alleging that the agency's demand for early license renewal on eight stations amounted to retaliation for coverage the president disapproved of, including the network's handling of late-night host Jimmy Kimmel. Also on Monday, a federal prosecutor sued over her termination, alleging retaliation for prior enforcement work, while the Justice Department appealed a judge's dismissal of charges against Kilmar Ábrego García — charges the judge himself had called "vindictive." In the Oval Office, Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it interfered with reopening the Strait of Hormuz, said he intended to declare the strait U.S. territory, and dismissed reports of poor conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought a legislative response to the weekend's self-dealing revelations. Senator Elizabeth Warren and nine colleagues introduced a bill to bar presidents, vice presidents, and senior officials from owning or controlling a bank — a direct answer to the World Liberty Financial charter. The Pentagon separately ordered thirty major universities, including Harvard, MIT, and Johns Hopkins, to sever foreign academic partnerships within two weeks or risk losing federal funding. The Justice Department announced it would deploy 1,000 election monitors to polling places for the midterms, citing unspecified voter-fraud concerns — a deployment far larger than the agency's historical practice. And Disney formally joined ABC's suit against the FCC, filing a complaint citing more than 600 document requests and describing a chilling effect on programming decisions; it was the first time in more than fifty years that a major broadcaster had faced this kind of early license review.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday offered one of the week's clearer instances of judicial pushback. The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed a preliminary injunction limiting immigration enforcement at Quaker, Sikh, and Baptist houses of worship, finding the administration's 2025 enforcement policy likely violated the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The same day, reporting surfaced describing Christian nationalists with influence in the administration advocating repeal of the Nineteenth Amendment in favor of household voting that would defer to men — a proposal aimed at over a century of constitutional suffrage protection. The week's pattern of attacks on the press also escalated: White House communications director Steve Cheung used vulgar insults against Senator Ossoff, Trump attached derisive nicknames to him, and the official White House rapid-response account attacked a CNN reporter by invoking her children.

**Thursday**

Thursday was the busiest day of the week and, in some ways, its clearest illustration of institutions pulling in opposite directions. Courts blocked two separate executive actions: a federal judge halted the transfer of 17 million commercial driver's license records to federal custody, and another blocked the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA from imposing DEI-related conditions on disaster-relief grants to Salem, Oregon, finding likely violations of separation of powers.

At the same time, the Justice Department defended its prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey, arguing in court filings that his seashell Instagram post could reasonably be read as a coded threat against the president — a prosecution his lawyers continue to call vindictive. Documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request showed FCC chair Brendan Carr working closely with the White House and right-wing media figures on license matters even as he oversaw renewal decisions affecting ABC. And reporting deepened on aide Natalie Harp, revealing she had worked at the White House for more than a year without a required security clearance while serving as a key filter of information reaching the president — a lapse that drew bipartisan concern from national security officials, regardless of the personal dynamics also being reported. Trump, meanwhile, gave the press a tour of extensive White House renovations that included materials donated by a campaign contributor, and separately staged a high-speed car race that required modifications to Washington's streets.

**Friday**

The week closed with a Supreme Court intervention that crystallized its earlier posture. Chief Justice Roberts stayed a lower court's order that had blocked construction of Trump's $400 million White House ballroom pending congressional approval, allowing the project to resume while the Court considers the underlying case — even though the appellate court had found the project likely required congressional sign-off.

The Pentagon, separately, fired the publisher, editor, and a reporter of Stars and Stripes, the military's own news outlet, for insubordination following its coverage of conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln and staff defense of editorial independence. The Department of Homeland Security dramatically retreated from its earlier claims about non-citizen voting, admitting after meeting with Nevada officials that it had manually confirmed only 185 non-citizens on the state's voter rolls — down from an earlier claim of nearly 16,000, itself a fraction of a national figure of roughly 278,000 the agency had floated. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent formally ended beneficial-ownership disclosure requirements under the 2021 Corporate Transparency Act, a law originally passed over presidential veto to combat money laundering. And federal budget cuts that reduced food-safety inspection capacity by more than 40 percent were linked to the largest cyclospora outbreak in U.S. history, as gas prices approached record highs and school lunch costs rose 11 percent.

**Assessment**

Read end to end, the week does not describe a single institution failing uniformly. It describes several institutions choosing differently under similar pressure. The Fourth Circuit limited enforcement at houses of worship; district courts blocked a data transfer and grant conditions built on shaky legal footing; the Supreme Court declined to revisit a jury's finding in the Carroll case. But the Attorney General publicly declined to promise independence, the FCC's chair coordinated with the White House against a network he regulates, and the Supreme Court's own stay let a presidential construction project proceed over an appellate court's constitutional concerns.

Alongside these institutional questions ran a due-process crisis in immigration courts, a foreign policy driven by threats and impulse rather than settled process, and a financial picture in which oversight tools were dismantled even as self-dealing surfaced in plain view. None of this occurred by accident; each instance involved a choice by a specific office or official. The record of who chose to check power, and who chose not to, is now part of the public account of how this period was governed. ```
Excerpt: This week's defining thread was the refusal of institutions meant to check the president to actually do so.
